title: Faithful Mobile GUI Agents with Guided Advantage Estimator
one_liner: Train a phone-screen agent to act only when the screen and the instruction support the action, then stabilize reinforcement updates so that faithful behavior does not disappear.
lead: GUI agents often look capable on normal tasks while still relying on shortcuts. They may tap a familiar button because they saw a similar screen before, not because the current screen and the user's request justify that tap. This paper treats that as the main failure. Faithful-Agent first teaches the model to refuse unsupported actions when evidence is perturbed, then uses a guided advantage estimator so that sparse rewards do not wash out the learning signal for grounded behavior.

problem.h2: Why GUI agents act without proper support
paras: A phone-use agent should read the visible screen, follow the written goal, and then choose the next action. In practice, many agents learn a weaker habit. They notice recurring layouts and jump to an action that often worked before. That shortcut can still score well on easy tasks, but it breaks as soon as a button moves, the text changes, or the instruction requires a careful check.

The training setup makes this worse because GUI rewards are sparse. Many action traces get nearly the same low score. When that happens, the update step cannot clearly distinguish a grounded action from a lucky shortcut. The paper's claim is that faithfulness must be taught directly and then protected during reinforcement learning.

callout.b: The paper's move in one sentence.
callout.html: Teach abstention when evidence is missing, then stabilize policy updates so that actions supported by the screen keep receiving stronger credit.

panels.title: 1. A task arrives on a phone screen
panels.viz_args: Instruction: open settings and disable notifications for one app.
panels.caption: The agent must use the visible screen and the user request together.

panels.title: 2. Shortcut behavior looks tempting
panels.viz_args: Agent taps a familiar location without checking the current evidence.
panels.caption: A memorized pattern can look successful because many apps reuse similar layouts.

panels.title: 3. Faithfulness training removes support
panels.caption: The model is trained to stop when the screen no longer supports the planned action.

panels.title: 4. Guided advantage rescales learning
panels.viz_args: Anchored update keeps useful differences visible even when rewards are similar.
panels.caption: The second stage protects the learning signal because sparse GUI rewards otherwise flatten the update.

panels.title: 5. Actions follow evidence
panels.caption: The trained agent acts only after the screen and instruction jointly support the choice.

steps.text: Show the model tasks where screen evidence or instruction support is deliberately weakened so that unsupported actions can be identified.
Teach the model to abstain or revise its plan when the visible evidence no longer supports the action.
For each GUI task, sample several action traces so that policy updates can compare stronger and weaker behaviors.
Use the guided estimator to keep relative differences visible because ordinary grouped updates can collapse when all rewards are similar.
Add a consistency score so that the written rationale and the chosen tap point reinforce one another.

paras: The paper changes the learning signal from generic task success to evidence-backed action choice. The model is no longer rewarded only for eventually reaching the target screen. It is trained to value the path where each action is justified by what is visible and by what the user asked for.
object.object: the action credit assigned to evidence-backed GUI behavior

hidden.name: whether the next action is genuinely supported by current evidence
paras: Faithfulness is not directly observable from the final success flag. An agent may reach the right page by accident, or it may fail while still following the evidence correctly. The hidden quantity is whether the chosen action is supported by the current screen and instruction at the moment it is taken.

Faithful-Agent makes that quantity easier to train because the first stage creates examples where support is intentionally removed. The model then learns that the correct response can be to stop or ask for clearer evidence. The second stage keeps that distinction alive during reinforcement learning because the guided estimator preserves differences that sparse rewards would otherwise blur.

heat.caption: The darkest cells mark the pieces the paper tries to preserve: screen support, instruction support, and a usable training signal for those distinctions.

reads.html: The key question is not only 'did the agent finish?' It is 'was this action justified by what the screen and instruction showed right now?'
The framework isolates groundedness and internal consistency, then keeps their credit signal visible during grouped policy optimization.

paras: Shortcut behavior survives because ordinary training often cannot tell grounded success from accidental success. If a GUI trace gets to the correct screen, the update may reward it even when several intermediate taps were unsupported. The faithfulness-first supervised stage attacks that problem directly by creating cases where unsupported behavior must be rejected.

The guided advantage estimator addresses a second failure. In grouped reinforcement learning, many traces can have nearly identical sparse rewards. Then the plain advantage values become tiny and unstable, so the update stops favoring the better grounded trace. The anchor-based tempering keeps a usable spread in the signal because it rescales updates relative to a reference inside the group.

The thought-action consistency reward closes the loop. A model that writes one plan and taps elsewhere is still unreliable. Rewarding alignment between explanation and action helps because the policy is pushed toward traces where both the written reasoning and the screen action point to the same evidence-backed choice.

stages.s: GUI task with screen observations and user instruction
Supervised faithfulness training on evidence-perturbed cases
Sample grouped action traces for each task
Rescale the grouped update with guided advantage tempering
Add consistency reward between stated plan and chosen action
A GUI agent that abstains from unsupported actions and acts from visible evidence

math.words: The total learning score combines task success, faithfulness support, and thought-action agreement, while the grouped update is rescaled so that near-tied rewards still produce a useful preference signal.
math.equation: total_score(trace) = task_score(trace) + alpha * support_score(trace) + beta * consistency_score(trace)
symbols: the value used to rank one GUI action trace during learning
how well the trace completes the requested GUI task
how strongly the chosen actions are supported by the visible screen and instruction
how well the model's stated plan agrees with the action it actually takes
weight on evidence support during learning
weight on thought-action agreement during learning

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Trace A reaches the target screen but uses one unsupported tap.
Its task score is 8, its support score is 2, and its consistency score is 2. With alpha = 1 and beta = 1, its total score is 12.
Trace B also reaches the target screen and every tap is supported by the visible labels.
Its task score is 8, its support score is 5, and its consistency score is 4, so its total score is 17.
The grouped update should prefer Trace B because it solves the task without relying on unsupported steps.

math.note: The paper uses a richer grouped reinforcement objective, but this summary captures the main idea that grounded action quality must remain visible during policy updates.

charts.title: Standard GUI agent training
charts.note: The baseline often reaches the goal on easy layouts but fails on trap tasks because it leans on shortcut behavior.

charts.title: Faithful-Agent
charts.note: The paper reports much stronger trap-case behavior because the agent is explicitly trained to reject unsupported actions.

items.b: Perturbations may miss real shortcut patterns.
items.html: If the evidence-removal stage does not create the kinds of traps that appear in real phone apps, the model may still learn unsupported habits on layouts that were never stressed during training.

items.b: Consistency reward can favor polished but wrong explanations.
items.html: A model can write a neat rationale that matches its tap while still reading the screen incorrectly, so consistency alone is not enough unless the support signal also stays strong.

items.b: Sparse rewards can still limit coverage.
items.html: If most rollouts fail very early, even a tempered grouped update may not provide enough information about which grounded behavior should be preferred next.
The method is most useful when trap-style evidence perturbations are realistic and when grouped updates still contain enough variation to separate grounded traces from shortcut traces.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a small Android-like benchmark with tasks such as changing a setting, muting one app, or editing a contact field. For each task, create ordinary screens and trap screens where a familiar location or icon is present but the supporting label is removed or changed.

Train one agent with ordinary supervised and grouped reinforcement learning and train a second agent with the Faithful-Agent procedure. Measure task completion on ordinary screens and faithful success on trap screens. Also log whether the agent abstains when support disappears, because that behavior is part of the target.
demo.metric_eq: faithful_gain = trap_success_faithful_agent - trap_success_baseline ; abstain_precision = correct_abstentions / all_abstentions
demo.closing: The demo should show that the better agent is not merely finishing more tasks. It should be acting from current evidence because that is the failure the paper sets out to fix.
